segments.text: Watch a pulse of light, just a few wave cycles long, race along a silicon wire toward a tiny ring.
segments.say: Watch a pulse of light, just a few wave cycles long, race along a silicon wire toward a tiny ring.

segments.text: Some of it hops into the ring, circles around and around, and leaks back out a little on every lap.
segments.say: Some of it hops into the ring, circles around and around, and leaks back out, a little on every lap.

segments.text: Every model so far was an approximation. This is Maxwell's equations themselves, solved on a grid. How?
segments.say: Every model so far was an approximation. This is Maxwell's equations themselves, solved on a grid. How?

segments.text: It's called finite-difference time-domain, FDTD, and it rests on two ideas: leapfrogging fields, and a border made of complex numbers.
segments.say: It's called finite difference time domain, F D T D, and it rests on two ideas: leapfrogging fields, and a border made of complex numbers.

segments.text: In two dimensions, the electric field E points straight out of the screen, and the magnetic field H lies flat in the plane.
segments.say: In two dimensions, the electric field, E, points straight out of the screen, and the magnetic field, H, lies flat in the plane.

segments.text: Maxwell's equations then say two things: a changing H is driven by the curl of E, and a changing E by the curl of H.
segments.say: Maxwell's equations then say two things. A changing H is driven by the curl of E, and a changing E, by the curl of H.

segments.text: The curl measures swirl: how much a field circulates around each point.
segments.say: The curl measures swirl: how much a field circulates around each point.

segments.text: Watch a bump of E. Its slopes make H start to circulate around it.
segments.say: Watch a bump of E. Its slopes make H start to circulate around it.

segments.text: That swirling H lowers E in the middle and raises it around the edge. The bump spreads into a ring: a wave that pushes itself along.
segments.say: That swirling H lowers E in the middle, and raises it around the edge. The bump spreads into a ring: a wave that pushes itself along.

segments.text: These rules contain only derivatives, which compare each point with its neighbours. Everything is local.
segments.say: These rules contain only derivatives, which compare each point with its neighbours. Everything is local.

segments.text: On a computer, sample the fields on a grid, and replace each derivative by a difference of neighbours.
segments.say: On a computer, sample the fields on a grid, and replace each derivative by a difference of neighbours.

segments.text: But that difference, divided by the spacing, gives the slope best at the midpoint between the samples, not at either end.
segments.say: But that difference, divided by the spacing, gives the slope best at the midpoint between the samples, not at either end.

segments.text: So in 1966, Kane Yee put H exactly at those midpoints: half a cell away from E.
segments.say: So in nineteen sixty-six, Kane Yee put H exactly at those midpoints: half a cell away from E.

segments.text: Time gets the same trick: E lives on whole time steps, and H on the half steps in between.
segments.say: Time gets the same trick. E lives on whole time steps, and H, on the half steps in between.

segments.text: The algorithm is a leapfrog. Use the curl of E to update H, then the curl of H to update E, and repeat.
segments.say: The algorithm is a leapfrog. Use the curl of E to update H, then the curl of H to update E, and repeat.

segments.text: Here it is in 1D, with real numbers: each new value uses only its two neighbours, yet the pulse marches on.
segments.say: Here it is in one D, with real numbers. Each new value uses only its two neighbours, yet the pulse marches on.

segments.text: Matter is just one number per cell, the permittivity ε. Any shape you can paint on the grid, you can simulate.
segments.say: Matter is just one number per cell, the permittivity, epsilon. Any shape you can paint on the grid, you can simulate.

segments.text: The grid has two rules of its own. First, a speed limit: each step, news travels only to neighbouring cells, so it spreads in a diamond.
segments.say: The grid has two rules of its own. First, a speed limit. Each step, news travels only to neighbouring cells, so it spreads in a diamond.

segments.text: Light spreads in a circle, which must fit inside the diamond: in 2D, c Δt ≤ Δx/√2. This is the Courant limit.
segments.say: Light spreads in a circle, which must fit inside the diamond. In two D, see delta tee, at most delta ex over root two. This is the Koo-rahnt limit.

segments.text: Break it by just six percent, and the computed field explodes.
segments.say: Break it by just six percent, and the computed field explodes.

segments.text: Second, the grid distorts waves. Recall the k-circle: in free space, all directions share one wavelength.
segments.say: Second, the grid distorts waves. Recall the kay circle: in free space, all directions share one wavelength.

segments.text: On the grid, the circle bulges, most along the axes: short waves travel too slowly, slowest along the grid lines.
segments.say: On the grid, the circle bulges, most along the axes. Short waves travel too slowly, and slowest along the grid lines.

segments.text: A pulse becomes a squarish ring, trailed by ripples. The fix: ten to twenty cells per wavelength, or more.
segments.say: A pulse becomes a squarish ring, trailed by ripples. The fix: ten to twenty cells per wavelength, or more.

segments.text: Now the hardest part: the grid must end somewhere, but real light just keeps going.
segments.say: Now the hardest part. The grid must end somewhere, but real light just keeps going.

segments.text: If the grid simply stops, its edge acts as a mirror, and the echo ruins the answer.
segments.say: If the grid simply stops, its edge acts as a mirror, and the echo ruins the answer.

segments.text: So add a layer that absorbs? A sudden change of material reflects too, right at its edge.
segments.say: So, add a layer that absorbs? A sudden change of material reflects too, right at its edge.

segments.text: A gentler layer must be thick and expensive. We need an absorber that light cannot see.
segments.say: A gentler layer must be thick, and expensive. We need an absorber that light cannot see.

segments.text: The trick, found in 1994 by Bérenger, and by Chew and Weedon, is to change not the material, but the coordinates.
segments.say: The trick, found in nineteen ninety-four by Berranjay, and by Chew and Weedon, is to change not the material, but the coordinates.

segments.text: Inside the border, let the position x pick up an imaginary part that grows with depth: x + (i/ω)∫σ dx.
segments.say: Inside the border, let the position ex pick up an imaginary part that grows with depth: ex, plus i over omega, times the integral of sigma.

segments.text: A wave e^(ikx) at this complex position keeps its wavelength, but gains a factor e^(−(k/ω)∫σ dx): it dies away.
segments.say: A wave, e to the i kay ex, at this complex position keeps its wavelength, but gains a factor, e to the minus kay over omega, times the integral of sigma. It dies away.

segments.text: These are the same Maxwell equations in stretched coordinates, so the border matches perfectly: no echo, at any angle or frequency.
segments.say: These are the same Maxwell equations, in stretched coordinates, so the border matches perfectly. No echo, at any angle, or frequency.

segments.text: This is the perfectly matched layer, or PML. Side by side: the wall echoes, the lossy layer echoes, the PML stays silent.
segments.say: This is the perfectly matched layer, or P M L. Side by side: the wall echoes, the lossy layer echoes, the P M L stays silent.

segments.text: On a grid, a tiny echo remains, so σ ramps up smoothly. Grazing and evanescent waves are the hardest to absorb.
segments.say: On a grid, a tiny echo remains, so sigma ramps up smoothly. Grazing and evanescent waves are the hardest to absorb.

segments.text: In code, the whole method is four lines inside a time loop.
segments.say: In code, the whole method is four lines inside a time loop.

segments.text: Update H from the curl of E. Update E from the curl of H. Absorb in the PML. Add the source.
segments.say: Update H from the curl of E. Update E from the curl of H. Absorb in the P M L. Add the source.

segments.text: Send in one short pulse, record what comes back, and a Fourier transform in time gives every wavelength from a single run.
segments.say: Send in one short pulse, record what comes back, and a Fourier-transform in time gives every wavelength, from a single run.

segments.text: For a Bragg mirror, a stack of alternating layers, the whole reflection spectrum lands right on the exact answer.
segments.say: For a Bragg mirror, a stack of alternating layers, the whole reflection spectrum lands right on the exact answer.

segments.text: The price: every cell is updated at every step. A small 2D run takes seconds; a large 3D device, minutes to hours on GPUs.
segments.say: The price: every cell is updated, at every step. A small two D run takes seconds. A large three D device, minutes to hours on G P U's.

segments.text: And it sees what simpler models miss: on this fine glass relief, the thin-element model sends 96% of the light one way. FDTD, with shadows and light trapped in the ridges, finds 57%.
segments.say: And it sees what simpler models miss. On this fine glass relief, the thin element model sends ninety-six percent of the light one way. F D T D, with shadows, and light trapped in the ridges, finds fifty-seven.

segments.text: FDTD isn't exact either: it converges as cells shrink, curves become staircases, and the PML adds a small error.
segments.say: F D T D isn't exact either. It converges as cells shrink, curves become staircases, and the P M L adds a small error.

segments.text: But the core idea is simple. E updates H, and H updates E, one neighbour at a time.
segments.say: But the core idea is simple. E updates H, and H updates E, one neighbour at a time.

segments.text: A layer of complex-stretched space absorbs whatever leaves.
segments.say: A layer of complex, stretched space absorbs whatever leaves.

segments.text: Now we can simulate almost anything. What we really want is the reverse: say what the light should do, and get the structure.
segments.say: Now we can simulate almost anything. What we really want is the reverse: say what the light should do, and get the structure.
